01 · Basics

A projection maps latitude and longitude on the sphere to x and y on the plane, and must stretch something on the way.

Scale factor

On Mercator the scale factor \( k = \sec\varphi \) grows towards the poles, so areas grow by \( k^2 \).

Worked example

At 72° N the formula above gives \( k = \sec 72^\circ \approx 3.24 \), so areas there are drawn \( k^2 \approx 10.5 \) times too large [1].

Go deeper: [1]

02 · Choosing

Use a conformal projection for navigation and local shapes; use an equal-area projection for anything that compares sizes.

Pitfall

Using Web Mercator for a world map of population density.

Go deeper: [1]

Check yourself

What does an equal-area projection keep?

  1. Shapes of small regions
  2. Relative sizes of regions
  3. Nothing
Equal-area keeps areas in proportion; it gives up shapes, which is what conformal projections keep.

Exercises

Exercise 1

On Mercator, by how much is area exaggerated at 60° latitude?

Hint 1

The area factor is the square of the scale factor.

Solution

k = sec 60° = 2, so areas are 2² = 4 times too large.
